title: Power Posing: Rise and Fall
objective: After this level you can trace how the power posing finding spread and weigh what replications later showed.
summary: A 2010 study said 'power poses' changed hormones and behavior, and a TED talk made it famous. Larger replications failed; only a small, debated effect on felt power remains.

cards.headline: Stand like a superhero for two minutes and change your hormones?
cards.body: That was the promise of power posing. It spread around the world. Then other researchers checked.

cards.headline: The rise
cards.body: In 2010 Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap had 42 people hold either expansive "high-power" poses or closed "low-power" ones, for one minute each. They reported that high-power poses raised feelings of power, testosterone and risk taking, and lowered the stress hormone cortisol. In 2012 Cuddy's TED talk on the idea became one of the most watched TED talks ever.

cards.headline: The fall
cards.body: In 2015 Eva Ranehill and colleagues tested power posing with 200 people. They found no effect on hormones or on risk taking, though people did report feeling more powerful. In 2016 the original lead author, Dana Carney, wrote: "I do not believe that 'power pose' effects are real." She called the original sample tiny and the data flimsy.

cards.headline: What's left, and why to be careful
cards.body: Later large analyses found one surviving effect: posture can shift how powerful people say they feel. The hormone and behavior effects are largely unsupported, and how much the felt-power effect means is still debated. Notice where it survived: a self-report. Carney also wrote that the original self-report measure was p-hacked: many power questions were asked, and the ones that "worked" were reported.

cards.headline: Power posing, weighed
learned: 2015: 200 people, no hormone or behavior effects
2016: the lead author said the effect isn't real
Left: a small, debated effect on felt power

questions.prompt: Put the power posing story in order, from earliest to latest.
items: Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap
questions.explanation: Carney, Cuddy and Yap published the original study in 2010, Cuddy's TED talk came in 2012, and Ranehill's team found no hormone or risk effects in 2015.

questions.prompt: Weighing the evidence, which summary of power posing fits best today?

options.label: Proven to change both hormones and bold behavior
options.rationale: Larger studies found no hormone or behavior effects.

options.label: Fully disproven, even for how people feel inside
options.rationale: A small effect on felt power remains, though it's debated.

options.label: It works, but only when held for over an hour
options.rationale: No study here tested anything like that.

options.label: Small, debated felt-power effect; no hormone or behavior effect

questions.explanation: The hormone and behavior claims failed to replicate; a small, debated effect on self-reported power is what's left.

questions.prompt: The one surviving effect is on how powerful people say they feel. Why does Level 8 urge caution with that kind of measure?

options.label: People can misremember or answer to look good
Self-reports can't be collected from large groups
options.rationale: Surveys collect them from many people easily.

options.label: Self-reports need hormone tests to count
options.rationale: They're a separate kind of measure.

options.label: Self-reports are banned by ethics boards
options.rationale: They're one of psychology's standard measures.

questions.explanation: Self-reports are useful but fallible, and Carney said the original self-report measure was p-hacked.
